payload.claim: The outer `except Exception as exc:` around `with mutate(mutant) as reason:` labels every exception raised by the context manager as a failed restore ("could not restore {mutant.file} after its mutant"), but `_mutated`'s `__enter__` half (via `apply_mutant`) can itself raise before anything is mutated — `apply_mutant`'s `target.write_bytes(new_content)` in saffron/mutation.py is not wrapped in a try/except the way the read is, so an OSError on write propagates through `mutate.__enter__`, is caught here, and is reported as a restore failure on a tree that was never actually mutated. This is a message-accuracy issue only (the status is still correctly `error` either way), so it does not change what the gate decides, but an operator reading "tree left mutated" for a tree that was never touched is being told something false about the data.
